replies.author: @minangaceh5263
replies.text:
Papua has been divided into six special autonomous provinces since 2022. No separatist group controls any territory there. Most of the people you mentioned, such as those associated with the Republic of West Papua, live in other Melanesian countries like Vanuatu. However, they do not have Indonesian citizenship and cannot freely enter Indonesia.

There are indeed conflict areas, particularly in the provinces of Highland Papua and Central Papua, but the conflict is very limited in scale. These armed groups have become increasingly weakened because the Indonesian military has cut off their weapons supplies, surrounded their positions, and restricted their movements since Papua was divided into six provinces, whereas previously it consisted of only two.

Journalists also face restrictions because they risk being kidnapped by separatist groups, as happened in the case of an American pilot. Therefore, restricting access to certain areas is considered a safer option.

Many former separatists have also surrendered and returned to Indonesian citizenship.

replies.author: @Cyfiero
replies.text:
​​​@GeographyNow You weren't wrong to not include Taiwan in this video. Taiwan, officially the Republic of China, is not just de facto independent from the People's Republic of China, but the two are also de jure separate. The ROC predates the establishment of the PRC. Although there is only one seat in the UN to represent China, despite popular misconception, the UN and international law does not in fact stipulate that membership in the UN determines sovereignty status. Notwithstanding all this, the ROC still constitutionally claims all of Mainland China (even though in practice they no longer desire to make true on this claim).
It is a case of two different states and governments laying de jure claim over one another and falls better into disputed territory category rather than the subject of your video. If you had included Taiwan, it would've necessarily biased Chinese nationalist narratives that are empirically and legally contested. 

Anyone commenting that the PRC and ROC belong to one country because of the "One China" principle is pushing a subjective, normative opinion. Yes, one can wish for a single Chinese ethno-state, but this is a personal ideal. The empirical reality as we would say in international relations is that the ROC and PRC are distinct governments which are sovereign states from one another, regardless of what people or other governments like to imagine "should" be the case.
